chunks: Al-Hasan ibn Ali al-Wassha narrated from Al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Faddal, from Abdullah ibn Bukayr, from Abdullah al-Lahham, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who buys the wife of a man from the People of Shirk (polytheism) to make her an Umm Walad (mother of a child by her master). He said, 'There is no harm in it.'

key_terms.أُمَّ وَلَدٍ: Umm Walad (a female slave who bears a child to her master)
key_terms.لاَ بَأْسَ: There is no harm / It is permissible

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on buying a polytheist woman who is already married to make her an Umm Walad?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, the Imam (AS) permits purchasing a slave woman married to a polytheist to become an *Umm Walad*, highlighting the flexibility of marital status in early Islamic jurisprudence. This ruling underscores the principle that the marriage of a slave woman to a non-Muslim does not necessarily prevent her from being acquired for concubinage, as the *Kitabah* or purchase effectively dissolves the existing bond or allows for it to coexist depending on the specific legal school's interpretation. It reflects the practical application of *Ahl al-Kitab* and *Ahl al-Shirk* distinctions in the context of slavery and family law during the Imamate period.
